content: 1. Administer 5 grams of piperacillin/tazobactam intravenously every 6 hours, totaling 18 grams per day (16 grams of piperacillin and 2 grams of tazobactam), for a duration of 7 to 14 days. Continue aminoglycoside therapy in specific cases as needed. 2. Avoid administering piperacillin/tazobactam in the absence of a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication, as this is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 3. When culture and susceptibility data are available, adjust or select antibacterial therapy accordingly. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns should guide empiric therapy selection. 4. Piperacillin/tazobactam is indicated for the treatment of appendicitis complicated by rupture or abscess and/or peritonitis in adults and pediatric patients aged 2 months or older, caused by beta-lactamase-producing isolates of Escherichia coli or specific members of the Bacteroides fragilis group (B. fragilis, B. ovatus, B. thetaiotaomicron, B. vulgatus). Safety and efficacy in patients under 2 months of age have not been established. 5. Piperacillin/tazobactam is also indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe nosocomial pneumonia in adults and pediatric patients aged 2 months or older, caused by beta-lactamase-producing isolates of Staphylococcus aureus, as well as piperacillin/tazobactam-susceptible isolates of Acinetobacter baumannii, Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. 6. Nosocomial pneumonia caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa may require a higher dose of 5 grams of piperacillin/tazobactam, and alternative formulations should be considered. 7. Piperacillin increases the effects of antithrombin alfa and antithrombin III through pharmacodynamic synergism. Avoid or use an alternative drug in such cases. 8. Piperacillin increases the anticoagulant effects of argatroban. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 9. Cephalosporins may decrease prothrombin activity, and caution is advised when co-administered with piperacillin. 10. Piperacillin decreases the effects of live bacterial vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine, through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live bacterial vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic treatment is completed, as antibiotics may reduce vaccine efficacy. 11. Piperacillin increases the anticoagulant effects of bivalirudin. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 12. Piperacillin can inhibit platelet aggregation, which may enhance the effects of anticoagulants like dalteparin, enoxaparin, and heparin. Avoid or use alternative drugs in such cases. 13. Piperacillin decreases the effects of oral microbiota products containing bacterial spores. Complete antibiotic regimens 2 to 4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. 14. Tetracyclines, such as omadacycline, sarecycline, and doxycycline, may interfere with the bactericidal action of piperacillin. Monitor for reduced therapeutic effects of piperacillin when used concomitantly with tetracyclines. 15. Piperacillin decreases the effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, camrelizumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab. Use caution and monitor closely, as co-administration may interfere with the therapeutic effects of these agents. 16. Piperacillin increases the toxicity of vancomycin. Monitor kidney function closely in patients receiving both drugs. 17. Piperacillin increases the effects of vecuronium, potentially prolonging neuromuscular blockade. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 18. Piperacillin and warfarin may enhance each other's effects through pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially causing platelet dysfunction. Monitor INR and adjust warfarin dosage as needed. 19. Piperacillin increases the effects of aminoglycosides, such as amikacin, gentamicin, neomycin, streptomycin, and tobramycin, through pharmacodynamic synergism. Monitor for potential toxicity. 20. Piperacillin interacts with aspirin and other salicylates (e.g., aspirin rectal, choline magnesium trisalicylate, willow bark) by competing for plasma protein binding sites, potentially enhancing the effects of displaced drugs. Monitor closely. 21. Piperacillin levels may be increased by diuretics such as chlorothiazide and hydrochlorothiazide, which decrease renal clearance. Monitor for potential toxicity. 22. Piperacillin increases the effects of ibuprofen IV, meclofenamate, and other acidic drugs by competing for renal tubular clearance. Monitor closely. 23. Piperacillin increases the effects of rose hips and sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering metabolism or renal clearance. Monitor for reduced efficacy of sodium picosulfate due to altered colonic bacterial flora. 24. Piperacillin increases the toxicity of vancomycin and vecuronium.
